description: Hi Team Proxima here to crack Nasa 2026
summary:
We built **SPHEREx Explorer**, a free web platform that allows anyone to search NASA’s new SPHEREx infrared all-sky survey for objects that move or change, using the same blink-comparison technique Clyde Tombaugh used to discover Pluto in 1930.

SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months in 102 infrared colors, but comparing these observations has not been easy. Our platform retrieves real SPHEREx Level-2 images from NASA/IPAC IRSA and enables users to blink, subtract, and stack observations, overlay Gaia stars and their proper motions, and flag and export potential candidates.

We also developed a machine-learning model trained on synthetic moving objects injected into 15 real SPHEREx fields. At a 1% false-alarm rate, it detects 68% of movers, compared to 46% using a simple rule-based approach.

Our motion measurements also closely match Gaia's reference data:

- Barnard's Star: 10.33″/yr (Gaia: 10.39″/yr)
- Epsilon Indi B: 4.53″/yr (Gaia: 4.68″/yr)

This opens up exciting possibilities for discovering cold brown dwarfs, nearby faint stars, and potentially even a distant "Planet X" that may be too faint or slow-moving for traditional visible-light surveys.

By turning SPHEREx's infrared observations into an accessible search platform, we're making astronomical discovery more approachable for students, researchers, and citizen scientists.
details:
SPHEREx Explorer is a web platform for finding moving and changing objects in NASA's SPHEREx infrared survey. Users can enter sky coordinates or select a benchmark target to explore real astronomical observations.

1. Fetches real data: Queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx Level-2 observations, downloads detector-specific image cutouts (D1–D6, 0.75–5 µm), and renders one frame per visit. Popular fields are cached for offline demonstrations.

2. Time Machine (WiseView for SPHEREx): Blinks observations using the same technique Clyde Tombaugh used to discover Pluto. Supports difference imaging, shift-and-add along trial motion, synthetic test objects, Gaia DR3 overlays with proper-motion vectors, and Pan-STARRS color references.

3. Sky Explorer: Displays astronomical images with coordinate grids, live RA/Dec readouts, FITS headers, image stretches, and customizable colormaps.

4. Spectral View: Visualizes SPHEREx's 102 spectral channels with markers for water, CO₂, CO, and methane ice features, helping distinguish cold brown dwarfs and icy objects from ordinary stars.

5. Discoveries: Allows users to flag candidates with motion measurements (″/yr), brightness changes (Δm), and notes, then export their findings as CSV for follow-up investigations, including Backyard Worlds.

6. AI Mover Model: Extracts 23 features per source, including motion significance, red/cyan difference-image pairs, brightness variation, object shape, and crowding. A stacked LightGBM + XGBoost classifier, optimized with Optuna, predicts the probability that a source is genuinely moving.

The model was trained on 1,367 synthetic movers and 1,358 static sources injected into 15 real SPHEREx fields, covering 60 visits and 300 stacks with realistic noise, blur, and crowding. Using leave-fields-out cross-validation and a threshold calibrated to a 1% false-alarm rate on 758 real Gaia stars, it recovered 68.0% of movers compared to 45.9% with a simple rule-based approach. The model and simulator are complete and are being integrated into the Time Machine.

Validation

Our motion measurements on real SPHEREx observations closely match Gaia reference measurements:

  • Barnard's Star: 10.33″/yr (Gaia: 10.39″/yr).
  • Epsilon Indi B: 4.53″/yr (Gaia: 4.68″/yr).

We also investigated real-world challenges, such as WISE 0855−0714 appearing just 1.4–9.6″ from a G = 16.3 star across all 168 exposures. These observations helped us develop crowding-aware features to reduce false positives.

Benefits and Impact

  • Makes a new NASA dataset accessible to students, amateur astronomers, and citizen-science communities without requiring installation or API keys.
  • Enables searches for nearby cold brown dwarfs, high-proper-motion stars, and distant Solar System objects, contributing to the modern Planet X search.
  • Uses AI-based ranking to reduce manual inspection while keeping every candidate independently verifiable through blinking.
  • Combines real astronomical observations, spectral analysis, and citizen-science workflows in one platform.

Tools and Languages

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Flask.
  • Frontend: React, Vite.
  • Astronomy: Astropy (FITS, WCS, coordinates), NumPy, SciPy, pandas.
  • Machine Learning: LightGBM, XGBoost, scikit-learn, Optuna.
  • Data Services: NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA and cutout services, ESA Gaia TAP service, Pan-STARRS image cutouts.
  • Viewer: Public-domain WiseView blinker (ASCL:1806.004), adapted for SPHEREx.
  • Hardware: No specialized hardware required.

Creativity

  • Adapted WiseView, a proven citizen-science tool from Backyard Worlds, for NASA's new SPHEREx mission, bringing the classic blink-comparator discovery technique into modern infrared astronomy.
  • Combined temporal motion detection with SPHEREx's unique 102-color spectral information to identify potential ice and methane signatures.
  • Addressed the rarity of moving objects by injecting synthetic movers into real SPHEREx images, training the model on realistic astronomical conditions, and evaluating its performance against real Gaia stars.
  • Integrated traditional astronomical techniques with machine learning while retaining human verification of every candidate.

Factors Considered

  • Scientific Honesty: Validates motion measurements against Gaia and labels findings as candidates rather than confirmed discoveries.
  • SPHEREx Limitations: Accounts for its 6.15″ pixels, meaning only sufficiently fast movers are distinguishable over a 1–2 year baseline. Crowding and blending are also considered potential sources of false motion.
  • Accessibility: Provides plain-language controls, shareable coordinates through URLs, and offline caching for popular fields.
  • Openness: Uses publicly available astronomical datasets and open-source technologies.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Based on the team's actual usage, select:

  • Code: Claude (Anthropic) assisted with writing and debugging portions of the code and scripts.
  • Text: Claude assisted with drafting documentation, presentation content, and project answers.
  • Images: Select only if AI-generated images were used in the presentation. Any such images must carry a visible "AI-generated" watermark.
